prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the active incretin peptide that enabled GLP-1-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the one candidate on which all six openings converge (five first places, one second). It is a complete arc from physiology to medicine: proglucagon processing, identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide, human incretin physiology and receptor biology, and then durable agonists that treat type 2 diabetes and obesity, with benefit now shown in large independent outcome trials, including cardiovascular and renal endpoints. The mechanism is independently confirmed over decades and the clinical impact is global and still growing, so recognition is neither premature nor contested on the science. I keep the Drucker, Holst, Mojsov trio because it covers three distinct basic-science steps (human physiology, receptor and tissue biology, peptide identity), which fits a prize for a discovery rather than for a product.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real. The three-person cap leaves out Knudsen, whose long-acting analogue design is what made the therapy work, and Habener and others who worked on proglucagon-derived peptides. A discovery-only trio may be criticised as honouring the biology while omitting the people who built the drugs, and Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is debated in the literature. If the committee judges this credit split unresolvable, a cleaner alternative such as the unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) or CAR-T would be more defensible on attribution grounds.

responses.point: Sandberg proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating Holst and Drucker as the physiological anchors and Knudsen as the pharmacological translation, with Mojsov's contribution acknowledged but sacrificed to the three-person cap.
responses.response: I take this seriously; it is not a trivial choice. The difference is whether the prize is for the biology of GLP-1 or for the drug. Knudsen's design of liraglutide and semaglutide is what turned a peptide with a minutes-long half-life into a therapy, and that is a real scientific achievement. But Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide is the step that made the physiology testable and the drug concept possible, and the Nobel tradition weights the discovery that opens a field. I therefore keep Mojsov, but I accept that the citation should name the therapeutic translation so that Knudsen's line is recognised in the text if not in the name list. Knudsen versus Mojsov is the key open question on this ballot.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks TNF blockade (Feldmann and Maini) first, citing a clean two-person attribution, more than two decades of independent evidence and a prize that is arguably overdue, with GLP-1 second.
responses.response: I agree that B001 has the cleaner attribution and is fully mature, so it is a genuine contender. But only she and Svenningsson ranked it at all (first and fifth), so it has little breadth of support, and I read the case as one of attribution tidiness rather than larger scientific or clinical consequence. TNF blockade defined a class of cytokine-targeted therapy for inflammatory disease, but GLP-1 has changed two very large disease areas and is still extending to cardiovascular and renal indications. Cleaner attribution should not decide the matter when the impact differs this much. I would not oppose B001 as a second part of a two-achievement prize, though under the three-person limit that would squeeze the GLP-1 laureates, which I would not want.

responses.point: Svenningsson, the chair, puts Knudsen alongside Drucker and Holst, arguing she is decisive for the long-acting analogues, and notes that credit among Mojsov, Habener and others is hard to settle.
responses.response: I agree that credit among Mojsov and Habener is difficult and I have not verified the priority record independently, so I hold my view with some uncertainty. My reservation about replacing Mojsov with Knudsen is that it shifts this from a discovery prize to a development prize while the basic-science credit is still being argued. I would want the committee to look at the documentary record on who first identified the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) and (7-37) forms before deciding. If that record proves unclear, your Drucker, Holst, Knudsen configuration becomes the safer choice and I would not block it.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) second and TOR (Hall alone) third, stressing mechanistic originality and compact attribution, and discounting the need for therapeutic translation in a basic discovery.
responses.response: I agree on the UPR: it is original and well confirmed, and Walter and Mori are a clean pair, which is why I rank it third and name it as an alternative. My qualification concerns medical consequence. This is the prize for Physiology or Medicine, and for the UPR the link to disease is still developing, so I would put it behind a candidate whose benefit to patients is already demonstrated. On TOR, Hall alone is defensible for the discovery, but I would want to understand why Schreiber and Sabatini are set aside, since their work on FKBP12-rapamycin and mammalian mTOR is not obviously secondary.

uncertainties: Whether the prize should credit only the basic discoverers (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov) or include Knudsen for the long-acting analogues, and who should be the third name if only two basic scientists are retained.
Mojsov's priority over Habener and others for identification of the active GLP-1 peptide, which I have not verified from primary documents.
Whether a two-achievement prize (GLP-1 plus B019 or B016) would force an unacceptable reduction of the GLP-1 laureate list under the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented connections (a 2019 review with Grillner, collaborations with Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons) involve no credited name. My neuroscience background is closest to B002 (optogenetics), which I do not propose, so no recusal is needed.
